  • collision stratum
  • spectator
  • differential module
  • cohomological shift
  • normal-transfer module

connection

A connection specifies how to differentiate or transport fields while respecting their gauge transformation law. On a line, it can be represented by a Lie-algebra-valued one-form.

Why it matters

The connection determines how a rotor history couples to the boundary gauge field.

Where it sits

Its parallel transport gives holonomy, while its variation measures the coupled gauge current.

Related

  • gauge transformation
  • holonomy
  • rotor

Connes operator

The Connes operator BB is the degree-one cyclic operation on Hochschild chains. Together with the Hochschild boundary it satisfies the mixed-complex identities.

Why it matters

A cyclic comparison must intertwine this operator as well as the ordinary boundary.

Where it sits

Under normalized Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg, it becomes the de Rham differential.

conservative functor

A conservative functor detects equivalences: if the image of a map is an equivalence, then the original map is one. For an exact functor of stable categories, it suffices that only the zero object maps to zero.

Why it matters

It states the positive detection property of the unbounded induced-module transform.

Where it sits

Conservativity does not assert that every target object is obtained or that all maps are recovered. Those are essential surjectivity and full faithfulness, respectively.

constant-perfect embedding

The constant-perfect embedding sends a perfect complex P to the constant inverse diagram with value P in the pro-perfect category. It preserves its cohomological degrees and maps.

Why it matters

It specifies the exact source of the unshifted direct four-position comparison, allowing coefficient duality to translate its mapping problem into an ordinary derived one.

Where it sits

This embedding is not coefficient transposition. Inverse coefficient duality sends the constant diagram of P to the dual complex, whereas it sends the coefficient transpose of P back to P.

constituent charge

Constituent charge counts the charged generators decorating a field state or current cochain. It is additive under products and can be preserved by the differential, translation and permitted maps.

Why it matters

It distinguishes a scalar vacuum class from the charged sector detected by a chosen current functional.

Where it sits

Four constituent variables can occur at one geometric position, and a four-position vacuum can have charge zero. A charge-four detector vanishes on a charge-preserving image of that vacuum.

constructible function

A constructible function on an algebraic variety takes finitely many values and is constant on the pieces of a finite algebraic stratification.

Why it matters

Constructible functions can be pulled through subobject correspondences and integrated using Euler characteristic.

Where it sits

The Hall functions used here are invariant under isomorphism and have the declared charge grading. Their convolution is defined from geometric subobjects.

contraction

A contraction in a free-field product is the scalar pairing contributed by two fields. Wick’s rule forms products by summing over allowed pairings. The contraction depends on the fields, their order, their separation and the chosen covariance.

Why it matters

It turns a covariance into explicit products on polynomial states.

Where it sits

This field-theoretic meaning differs from a homotopy contraction, which retracts a complex onto a simpler one.

convolution

Convolution combines products over decompositions. For a coalgebra (C,Δ)(C,\Delta) and an algebra (A,μ)(A,\mu), maps f,g:C→Af,g:C\to A have f∗g=μ(f⊗g)Δf*g=\mu(f\otimes g)\Delta, where the tensors and sums are defined. Function convolution on ℝ\mathbb R is (f∗g)(u)=∫f(v)g(u−v)dv(f*g)(u)=\int f(v)g(u-v)\,dv. Geometric convolution takes an external tensor product, pulls it to a correspondence and pushes it to its output. Its correspondence, coefficient category, support and inverse/direct-image conventions specify the product.

Why it matters

Collision convolution combines coefficient systems at disjoint configurations. Function convolution forms the arithmetic test algebra. Both retain the data over which composition occurs.

Where it sits

Noether convolution uses coalgebra decompositions of inputs. Collision convolution additionally retains geometric extension and restriction maps. Fourier transform converts additive function convolution to pointwise multiplication; that formula alone does not define the other two products.

convolution centre

Let 𝒞\mathcal C be the presentable stable collision coefficient category with its symmetric disjoint-configuration convolution ⋆\star, preserving colimits in each variable. For an associative algebra AA in 𝒞\mathcal C, its convolution centre Z(A)Z(A) represents V↦MapA-A⁡(V⋆A,A)V\mapsto\operatorname{Map}_{A\text{-}A}(V\star A,A), where the maps preserve both AA-actions.

The compatible composition operations give Z(A)Z(A) an E2E_2-algebra structure. Evaluation is final among coherent convolution actions on AA. Here such an action is a module structure on AA in the category of associative algebras in 𝒞\mathcal C.

Where it sits

The whole configuration coefficient system is retained; its empty component is only the scalar centre. The E2E_2 and finality statements use this symmetric convolution category and the stated coherent actions. A nonsymmetric consecutive-word product or an action through the diagonal tensor defines a separate problem.

coproduct

A coalgebra coproduct is a linear map Δ:C→C⊗C\Delta:C\to C\otimes C. It is coassociative when (Δ⊗1)Δ=(1⊗Δ)Δ(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta, and a counit ϵ:C→k\epsilon:C\to k satisfies (ϵ⊗1)Δ=(1⊗ϵ)Δ=idC⁡(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=\operatorname{id}_C. In an ordinary bialgebra, Δ\Delta also preserves multiplication with the usual tensor product. The word has a second categorical meaning: a coproduct ∐iXi\coprod_iX_i is a universal recipient of maps from all XiX_i; for vector spaces it is their direct sum.

Coalgebra coproducts split insertion data and become products after coefficient duality. Their compatibility with multiplication distinguishes possible quantum-group structures.

A braided or spectral coproduct uses its specified interchange and coefficient domain. Categorical coproducts occur instead in statements about direct sums, compactness and totalizations; the two meanings are determined by the displayed maps.

For a connected coaugmented coalgebra, the coradical filtration measures how many iterated reduced coproducts are needed to kill an element. Its first positive layer consists of the unit together with primitive elements.

Its graded pieces inject into tensor powers of the primitive space, allowing local finiteness of translation on unit extensions to propagate to all coefficients.

If the primitive space has dimension d, the nth filtered piece has dimension at most one plus d through d to the nth power in the stated connected setting.

A cotangent theory pairs fields with conjugate fields, as coordinates pair with covectors in a cotangent bundle. Its action couples the conjugate fields to equations for the original fields.

The pairing makes free differentials, contractions and boundary variations explicit.

Powers of ψi\psi_i define gravitational descendant insertions.

counit

A counit is a map ε:C→K\varepsilon:C\to K from a coalgebra to its tensor unit such that applying it to either output of the coproduct recovers the original input. For a Hopf algebra it is also a unital algebra map.

Why it matters

Counits remove empty pieces from a decomposition and provide the unit identities in tensor and cotensor comparisons.

Where it sits

A field-preserving scalar map, a covariant counit, a local vacuum state, and an augmentation are different conditions. In a spectral level family, the canonical covariant counit occurs at the identity level.

A Cousin complex assembles local cohomology along the strata of a filtration of a space, with differentials connecting successive supports. It is a Cousin resolution when its augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism.

It retains the partition diagonals, normal derivatives and merger residues of finite collision coefficients.

Its supported differential need not be an associative binary product. The actual resolution and its coalgebra operations require their own compatibility proof.

critical coefficient

A critical coefficient is the constructible complex obtained by gluing local vanishing-cycle complexes of an oriented d-critical space or stack. The orientation includes a square-root line with its square map. Smooth-atlas comparisons and their relative-dimension shifts are part of the gluing.

It is the coefficient object pulled through extension correspondences to define a critical Hall product.

The critical level of a simple affine current algebra in the stated normalization is minus h∨. It is the fixed point of the pairing involution sending kappa to minus kappa minus 2h∨.

At this level, a paired vacuum kernel can retain positive-weight classes whose contraction away from criticality divides by kappa plus h∨.

It differs from the single-module uncurved level minus 2h∨. Level variation on critical cohomology is measured by the level Bockstein.

The critical locus of a function WW is the locus where its differential vanishes. Its derived version is the derived intersection of the differential graph with the zero section of the cotangent space.

The crossed field tensor V1⊠ρV2V_1\boxtimes_\rho V_2 is the ordinary tensor module of two covariant field algebras, with a field product corrected by a spectral pairing when the second input row passes the first. Its coaction coefficient is the reversed product of the two coaction coefficients.

It is the field algebra that receives the spectral level-changing coproduct and acts on tensor products of covariant modules.

A cup product combines cochains using a diagonal on a resolution and multiplication in their coefficients. For Hochschild cochains, it cuts a bar word into two pieces and evaluates one cochain on each piece, with the graded tensor sign.

On the two-sided bar it represents derived composition. It also determines the binary operation represented by the square of a central character.

current

A current is an operator field associated with a symmetry or its charge. Its Laurent coefficients are operators called modes. Their commutators are determined by the singular terms in products of currents.

Currents give explicit examples in which a collision determines an algebra of symmetries.

A single Heisenberg current has a scalar double pole. Affine currents can also have a simple pole carrying a Lie bracket.

A curved A-infinity coring over H has higher coproducts of degrees 2 minus their output length, with outputs balanced over H. The zero-output map is curvature. Their identities say that the corresponding differential on the relative cobar tensor algebra squares to zero.

It retains every word-length component created when a small current resolution is deformed, including a ternary coproduct arising from a cubic differential.

The cut product combines coefficient systems by summing over consecutive cuts of an ordered word. d-critical structure

A d-critical structure records, on a classical space or stack, compatible local presentations as the critical loci of functions on smooth spaces. It retains the critical function to the order needed for its canonical line and vanishing-cycle constructions. It does not determine the entire derived enhancement.

It carries critical coefficient and orientation information on a classical moduli stack even when different derived recipients have not been globally identified.

For a smooth stack BB, the zero function gives the zero d-critical structure. Its canonical line is KB⊗2K_B^{\otimes2}, with canonical orientation root KBK_B. The associated oriented critical coefficient is ℚB[dim⁡B]\mathbb Q_B[\dim B], using smooth-stack descent and rational Betti coefficients.

A quantum field theory describes quantum observables and their dependence on where they are inserted. The products of nearby observables contain the interactions and symmetries that a dual description must retain.

The Todd class is the characteristic class with factor x/(1−e−x)x/(1-e^{-x}) for each Chern root xx of a complex vector bundle. It appears in Riemann–Roch formulas.

Its square root corrects the pairing in the Hochschild-to-Hodge state comparison.

Tor group

A Tor group is the homology in a specified degree of a derived tensor product. It records the failure of ordinary tensor product to be exact; it can be computed by resolving one input by flat or projective modules.

Why it matters

It retains the extra fibre and fusion classes that ordinary coefficient substitution can lose.

Where it sits

Flatness over the scalar ring does not imply flatness over an algebra through which two modules are balanced.

torsion

Over a domain RR, an element of a module is torsion if some nonzero element of RR annihilates it. For a specified ideal, ideal-torsion instead means that some power of that ideal annihilates the element.

Why it matters

Parameter torsion retains integral collision information, while ideal-torsion characterizes the finite-normal coefficient objects.

Where it sits

These meanings specify different coefficient conditions. Neither is automatically the same as topological support on a closed set.

torsor

A torsor for a group is a space locally carrying a free transitive group action, without a chosen identity point.

It lets extension endpoints live on one common elliptic curve.

Where it sits

A product over the classifying stack retains the identification of their torsors.

trace-class operator

A trace-class operator is an operator on a Hilbert space whose singular values have finite sum. Its trace is well-defined and independent of the orthonormal basis.

Why it matters

The heat operator must be trace class for the thermal partition function to be finite.

Where it sits

Trace-class control is an analytic condition beyond formal Hamiltonian expressions. Local nuclearity or square summability alone does not establish it on the stated Hilbert space.

The two-sided bar of a right A-module M and a left A-module N has terms consisting of M, a word of A entries, and N. Its differential combines internal differentials, adjacent multiplications and both endpoint actions. Its derived totalization computes the tensor of M and N over A.

Keeping both endpoints makes interface composition and the coring diagonal explicit.

Deconcatenation retains every cut, including the empty prefix and suffix. Omitting endpoint terms can destroy the chain identity and the unit for composition.

A unipotent tensor category in this setting is a finite-length abelian tensor category whose only simple object is the unit. Every object is built by successive extensions of the unit.

Why it matters

Unit self-extensions then control the primitive part of the coefficient coalgebra and provide the spectral regularity test.

Where it sits

Exact tensor products make composition lengths multiplicative. Unipotence does not force the coefficient coalgebra to be cocommutative or translation to have only finite orbits.

The Vandermonde polynomial in roots x1,…,xnx_1,\ldots,x_n is ∏i<j(xj−xi)\prod_{i\lt j}(x_j-x_i). Its square is symmetric and vanishes where two roots coincide.

Multiplication by the squared Vandermonde gives the explicit comparison between the two even shuffle products.

Its factorization into within-block and cross-block factors proves compatibility in every charge. Inverting it removes the root-collision locus.

Critical Hall operations must transport the coefficients of their actual potential.

Compactly supported dimensional reduction is a pushforward theorem; it does not identify every restricted vanishing-cycle sheaf with a constant sheaf.

variational derivative

A variational derivative of a functional is the coefficient of a field variation after integration by parts. For local functionals it is generally a distribution. Odd field variations require a specified left or right derivative convention.

It determines the conjugate-field source and Hamiltonian action of a boundary observable.

A distributional variation need not be a smooth tangent vector before heat regularization.

vector space

A vector space over a coefficient field is a collection whose elements can be added and multiplied by scalars, satisfying the linearity laws. A linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication.

States, coefficients and infinitesimal variations begin as vector spaces before products and differentials are added.

Where it sits

A topology, grading or completion supplies additional structure and can change which linear maps are allowed.

Verdier duality is the geometric contravariant duality that exchanges direct-image and exceptional-extension operations. For bounded holonomic differential-module complexes it is involutive; an open immersion satisfies j!=𝔻j∗𝔻j_!=\mathbb D j_*\mathbb D on that domain.

Applied to a bar coalgebra, it produces an associative algebra for the convolution with dualized geometric functors.

A vertex algebra is a vector space VV with a vacuum 𝟏\mathbf1, translation TT, and fields Y(a,z)b∈V((z))Y(a,z)b\in V((z)). The vacuum creates translated states, translation differentiates fields, and locality and associativity compare their singular products. It records all coefficients of local field products, not only a mode Lie bracket.

Heisenberg and affine current algebras provide examples. Quantum vertex algebras retain a specified exchange operator.

vertex coalgebra

A vertex coalgebra has a counit, a translation operator and mode coproducts satisfying the identities dual to those of a vertex algebra. A graded continuous dual gives such a structure when every transposed mode lands in the declared tensor product.

It retains the regular and singular coefficients of the completed fields under duality.

Its mode coproducts differ from deconcatenation in an associative bar. The continuous dual here has finite weight and finite character-jet support.

A vertex ideal is a submodule stable under all left and right field modes and the required translation operators.

Its modules retain conformal descendants and provide the independent full-state realization of an arithmetic fusion category.

A highest-weight vector is killed by all positive modes and is an eigenvector of the zero mode. Negative modes generate its descendants, subject to the relations of the chosen irreducible quotient.
